channel.title: EverythingTech
channel.description: A daily tech newspaper. 45+ sources, read in full and edited by an LLM every morning.

item.title: Nvidia's board weighs ousting Jensen Huang after a second affair report
item.description:
The board has hired a former federal prosecutor to investigate, while Trump says the FBI is looking into an alleged Chinese spy link.

Nvidia's board is set to hold urgent talks about whether its founder and chief executive should stay, after two people familiar with the matter said Huang had a romantic relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company's vice-president of healthcare and an 18-year veteran. The reports, first carried by The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal, sent Nvidia's shares down more than 8% in after-hours trading. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment, and Powell could not be reached.

The new report lands on top of a bigger problem. Huang acknowledged an affair on Sunday, two days after the Financial Times linked him to Alice Huang, an executive at one of Nvidia's customers, and US intelligence reportedly believes she was also tapped by Chinese state security. The board launched a probe and this week brought in a former prosecutor to run it, yet it still stood behind Huang as CEO on Sunday. According to Trump, the FBI is looking into the matter, and lawmakers in both parties want hearings.

What is still open is whether the board acts before its investigation reports. The Wall Street Journal describes the board as weighing a removal, not as having decided one, so the Wednesday meeting is the first point where a change could be announced. The stakes go beyond Nvidia's stock. Huang has become an influential voice in the president's circle on AI policy and export controls, so any change at the top would be felt in Washington as well as in the markets.

item.title: AWS releases a free, open-source emulator that runs AWS APIs on your laptop
item.description:
Tests and coding agents talk to a local HTTPS endpoint at no charge, and you pay for AWS resources only once you deploy.

AWS has released AWS Emulator, a local emulator that runs on a developer's machine and answers the same API calls as the cloud. The AWS CLI, the AWS SDKs, and coding agents reach it over a local HTTPS endpoint, so existing tests and scripts keep their code and only their endpoint settings change. The emulator is free, and its source is on GitHub. On Linux it installs from an RPM or Debian package, while macOS and Windows users run it in Docker from a Dockerfile in the documentation.

The design choice that matters is fidelity. The emulator is written in Rust to keep CPU and memory use low on a laptop, and it is built from the same AWS API models the SDKs use, so requests and error responses should have the same shape as the real service. On start, it generates its own credentials, a config file, and a certificate in a directory under ~/.aws, then binds to 127.0.0.1 so only the local machine can reach it. That makes it practical for a coding agent to create resources, check the results, and retry without waiting on a deployment to a region.

Coverage is the main limit. The emulator supports services that have an API model in AWS's public repository, so the value depends on whether your code uses only those services. It is also a test tool rather than a copy of the cloud, so behaviour that depends on the live account is still a deployment question. Teams should confirm their services are supported before moving CI onto it.

item.title: Gemini 4 Carbon reaches all paying developers at $2 and $10 per million tokens
item.description:
Carbon is aimed at the hardest multi-step coding and research work, while Google still recommends the cheaper Argon model for most tasks.

Gemini 4 Carbon now reaches every paying developer and enterprise customer, accessible by API from Google AI Studio and from Gemini for business. The price matches Argon's introductory rate: $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. Carbon was first offered to a set of cyber defenders two weeks ago. Google AI Ultra subscribers get it across Antigravity, the Gemini app, and AI Mode in Search.

Google positions Carbon above Argon. Argon stays the choice for most software engineering and knowledge work. Carbon uses more tokens to explore, reason, and run extended verification loops, which suits complex debugging and open-ended scientific work. Google says Carbon ranks first on CursorBench 4.0, Perplexity's WANDR, and Zapier's AutomationBench, at more than twice lower cost per task than the next-best external model. Those are Google's own figures, so they should be checked against your own tasks.

The release also previews /swarm in Google Antigravity, which turns one prompt into a team of agents working in isolated workspaces. In that setup Carbon takes the architecture, coordination, and auditing roles, lighter models handle parallel work, and adversarial verifier agents test each change. Whether a multi-agent run on Carbon ends up cheaper than one long run depends on how many tokens the team spends, and Google has not published that comparison.

item.title: For the first time, a C++ standard draft reportedly fails its national body vote
item.description:
Two approval thresholds were reportedly missed, and 12 countries abstained, a sign the C++26 draft is still contested.

The C++26 draft appears to have failed the national body ballot, the final step before ISO sign-off. The account, carried in a Lobsters post that cites a LinkedIn post by Robert Seacord and a comment by J. Daniel García, says the draft missed both bars: fewer than two-thirds of participating voters said yes, and more than a quarter voted no. It also says 12 countries abstained, some because they could not reach a common position. The account rests on social media posts, so the official tally is still needed.

The reason this matters is the process. National bodies are meant to confirm a draft that the standards committee, WG21, has already settled, so a failed ballot suggests contested features reached the working draft. The Lobsters author says that is a sign of division in the community whatever a reader thinks of the outcome, and that the ISO process is slow and hard to follow from outside the committee.

What is still open is the committee's next move. It now has to resolve the disputed items, and the official ballot comments will show which features drove the votes. Until those are published, the scale of the disagreement is an inference from the reported numbers.

item.title: CoreWeave shifts to customer prepayments and short contracts to fund its buildout
item.description:
Revenue rose 168% to $3.66 billion, but a $709 million net loss and a $132.5 billion backlog make the financing choices the story.

CoreWeave, which leases GPU capacity to AI developers, is changing how it funds its expansion. On its third-quarter earnings call, the company described collecting payment earlier from customers, borrowing against individual contracts, and signing shorter agreements that can command higher rates. Revenue reached $3.66 billion, up 168% from a year earlier, though the company also booked a $709 million net loss and $846 million of quarterly interest expense.

The shift is a response to the cost of debt. Intrator told analysts the company has no plan to fund itself with unsecured bonds while yields stay this high. Instead it intends to borrow against specific customer contracts and draw the money as construction needs it, covering most of the buildout still ahead of a $132.5 billion backlog. CoreWeave projects roughly $9 billion of customer prepayments and deposits in the next three months, over $3 billion of it from signing new contracts for capacity already built.

Pricing is the other lever. CoreWeave raised prices about 25% in July and another 10% later in the quarter, and it says prices are still rising enough to more than offset cost increases. Short-term capacity sells above $40 million per megawatt a year, against $20 million to $25 million for new four- and five-year contracts. Prepayments commit the company to services at today's terms, which could look low if compute demand softens. Rivals Nebius and IREN have also relied on large Microsoft prepayments, which suggests the industry is pushing the cost of buildouts onto its biggest customers.

item.title: GitHub Agentic Workflows reaches general availability with default spending caps
item.description:
Coding agents run inside Actions with read-only defaults and a $10 cap per run, but the protections stop short of custom write jobs.

GitHub has made Agentic Workflows generally available, a project that runs coding agents inside GitHub Actions for tasks such as issue triage and analysing failed CI runs. Workflows are written in Markdown with YAML frontmatter and compiled into standard Actions workflows, so they reuse existing runner groups and policies. Agents start with read-only permissions, and proposed changes are applied by separate jobs that hold their own write tokens. A threat-detection job scans those changes before they land.

Spending is capped by default. Each AI Credit costs $0.01, and a single run is limited to 1,000 credits, which is $10. Enterprise defaults add a ceiling of 5,000 credits per day, 400 per threat-detection run, and a 20-minute limit on the agent step, and organisations can raise any of them. A forecast command estimates monthly spend. The safeguards are narrower than the headline suggests, though: the project's FAQ says they do not automatically cover direct write permissions or custom jobs that a workflow author adds.

The project also has a security trade-off in self-hosted setups. Its Actions Runner Controller support runs Docker-in-Docker as a privileged sidecar by default, so the agent's sandbox containers depend on a privileged component. One engineer at freenet, testing an issue-triage workflow, judged the default budget far too generous and capped his runs at 100 credits, 15 turns, and 10 minutes. Teams adopting it should set their own budgets before enabling a workflow and review custom write jobs by hand.

item.title: Nvidia donates OpenShell agent-security runtime to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation
item.description:
OpenShell applies fixed policy to what agents do with tools, and Nvidia is also contributing to a Google-led framework for long-running agents.

Nvidia has contributed OpenShell, an open runtime that secures and oversees autonomous AI agents, to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation as a CNCF Sandbox project. Under that arrangement the project will be governed by the organisations building it into their products rather than by Nvidia alone. Nvidia is also contributing to Agent Substrate, a Google-led framework for running long-lived agent workloads on Kubernetes, which the CNCF has accepted into its Sandbox as well.

OpenShell's job is policy enforcement. According to Nvidia, it imposes fixed rules on agent actions, so teams can set policy for tool use, access to inference services, and workload execution. The design is extensible, letting teams plug in their own compute, inference providers, credential stores, and monitoring. Nvidia reports hundreds of adopters, and the project has drawn tens of thousands of contributions in its first year.

Two things remain open. Donation to a foundation changes who governs the project, but whether outside maintainers gain real control over its roadmap depends on how the Sandbox stage develops. The security value also depends on how independent reviewers examine the code, and the announcement is the vendor's own account.

item.title: Google finds stale code comments send coding agents on unrequested side quests
item.description:
In sessions where the detours happened, agents used 77% more tokens and took 105% more wait time, according to Google's regression analysis.

Google engineers Sam Saccone and Madhuri Garikapati describe a failure they call agent distraction. AI coding agents read leftover task markers, obsolete bug references, and outdated specs in a codebase, then pursue them without being asked. In traces covering thousands of engineers and hundreds of millions of agent steps, about 13% of sessions exposed agents to inline references of that kind. Agents acted on the referenced bug in 6% of those cases, and the prompt rarely mentioned that bug.

Of those unprompted detours, 41% were on tickets already closed, and 57% were on open bugs outside the scope of the developer's request, which the authors classed as scope creep. The cost is measurable. A regression with clustered standard errors found the detours added 70% more steps, 77% more tokens, and 105% more wait time per session. At worst, the authors say, agents can be led to incorrect logic and decisions.

Google's fix was scanner agents that check each comment against bug status and the user's prompt, opening removal pull requests only after confirming an obsolete reference. Some scanners had to read years of git history to be sure. Over six months the cleaner removed thousands of stale references with more than 95% acceptance from human reviewers. The paper's remedies are codebase hygiene, including presubmit analysers and scanners, rather than a change in the models themselves.

item.title: United bans personal AI agents from booking its flights
item.description:
United cites credential security and federal rules on in-person verification, and it is restricting access through its own sites and through travel agencies.

United Airlines has barred personal AI assistants from making reservations on travellers' behalf. The airline said it is restricting access directly on its digital platforms and indirectly through travel agencies and aggregators, and it is updating its booking and ticketing policies to match. Its reasons are security and compliance. An agent that books a flight needs a traveller's credentials and payment details, and United warns that such tools could make unintended purchases, change accounts, or use MileagePlus miles.

United also argues that some tasks, such as checking in through an AI agent, could break federal rules that require travellers to confirm in person that their luggage contains no banned substances. The analyst Henry Harteveldt reads the policy as control over the sales channel. AI agents would add another intermediary on top of search engines, metasearch sites, and online travel agencies, and each flight search costs the airline money.

Other carriers are taking a different approach. Southwest has made its flight inventory viewable to ChatGPT users. United fares will still be sold through Kayak, Hopper, and Google Flights. Harteveldt also notes that blocking the bots will not make United fares any easier to find. What is unresolved is whether a rule aimed at consumer agents holds up as those tools become standard.

item.title: Appeals court limits a Justice Department demand for journalists' LinkedIn messages
item.description:
The unanimous panel said the demand covering 18 months of messages from journalists with no link to the leak probe went too far, and it ordered the request narrowed.

A three-judge federal appeals panel ruled that the Justice Department's leak investigation cannot sweep up the confidential sources of journalists who have no connection to it. The department had asked LinkedIn for 18 months of communications from targeted journalists, who together published more than 1,000 articles on many topics. The request was not limited to reporters tied to the report at the centre of the investigation. It reached anyone with a possible link to them.

LinkedIn challenged the order. The court refused to quash it entirely but told the district court to narrow it substantially, because the request posed a grave threat to press freedom. Writing for the unanimous panel, Judge J. Harvie Wilkinson III said security and free speech can coexist. A secrecy order had also barred LinkedIn from disclosing the request for a year, which the judges said left journalists unaware for far too long that their rights might be affected.

The ruling leaves the shape of the narrowed order to the district court. LinkedIn's argument was that most journalists publish contact details so sources can reach them, which makes broad requests a threat to a channel reporters use to meet confidential sources. The terms of the narrowed order, and whether the government seeks further review, are the next things to watch.

item.title: Fractile raises $720 million for an AI chip built on stacked DRAM
item.description:
The round, led by Thrive Capital, values the British company above £5 billion, and the company says its first chips ship next year.

Fractile, a British startup building AI chips, has raised a $720 million Series C led by Thrive Capital, Founders Fund, Lightspeed Venture Partners, and Redpoint, with backing from Britain's Sovereign AI Fund. The government puts the valuation at over £5 billion, which the Financial Times and a Reuters source have reported as possibly about $7 billion. Fractile presents itself as a frontier AI company rather than a chip vendor, and it is building a machine learning compiler alongside its hardware to speed up LLM execution.

The hardware bet is on memory. After a pivot, Fractile's design uses DRAM stacked on top of each chip, with the aim of avoiding the usual trade-off between memory capacity and speed. That trade-off matters more as agentic systems chain long sequences of tasks through large models, because compute is already struggling to keep up with demand.

Fractile's CEO Walter Goodwin wrote on LinkedIn that a lot of work remains, and the new funding is meant to let the company ship its first chips and systems next year. It is among the best-funded players in a field that includes Axelera, Etched, and OLIX. The test is whether the stacked-memory design reaches customers on schedule.

item.title: Angular's Rust-based compiler preprocessor enters beta, with 2x to 3x faster cold builds in one benchmark
item.description:
The compiler exists because TypeScript 7's Go rewrite removed the Transformer API that Angular's ahead-of-time compiler relied on.

The Angular team has released a beta of ngp, the Angular Preprocessor. It moves the analysis stage of the compiler into Rust, built on Oxc, the Rust toolchain from VoidZero that also powers Vite. The trigger was TypeScript 7.0: Microsoft's Go-based rewrite dropped the Transformer API that Angular's ahead-of-time compiler relies on. The older ngc compiler wrapped tsc and leaned on that API to convert decorators into runtime code. The Go port has no workable substitute, since crossing the JavaScript-Go boundary for every file would be too slow.

ngp works in three stages. A Rust frontend finds Angular declarations and resolves their metadata in parallel. The existing TypeScript template compiler then emits a runtime file and a type-check block file, and a downstream tool such as tsgo, tsrs, esbuild, or Rolldown handles type checking and emission. In a benchmark by Cédric Exbrayat of Ninja Squad across three projects of 15 to 1,714 components, the beta delivered a 2x to 3x speedup on cold builds, and peak memory on the largest project fell from 2.8 GB to 1.4 GB.

A separate prototype, vite-plugin-ngp by Christopher Holder, compiles files on demand. On a 252-component codebase, its dev server showed the first page after 10.5 seconds, versus 17.4 for ng serve, although Holder describes it as a prototype on a prototype pinned to a pre-release. Three projects is a small sample, so the numbers are signals rather than guarantees. Whether the beta holds up on large production apps is the open question.

item.title: JioHotstar finds plain code search wins clear tasks, while semantic retrieval helps ambiguous ones
item.description:
Six retrieval approaches were tested with Claude Sonnet, and adding retrieval layers did not reliably cut token use or raise completion rates.

Engineers at JioHotstar tested six code-retrieval options for coding agents: plain filesystem tools, Sourcebot, Graphify, CocoIndex Code, Repowise, and an in-house RAG pipeline. The tests combined public benchmark subsets with an internal question-answering setup built on the company's own repositories, using Claude Sonnet as the model doing the work.

On concrete tasks the plain filesystem baseline stayed competitive. Sourcebot, which offers indexed search, symbol definitions, and references, beat the baseline on harder SWE-bench Verified tasks while costing less. On simpler tasks, retrieval mostly added overhead. CodeScaleBench showed the reverse pattern. Semantic retrieval helped when problem descriptions were ambiguous and had to be mapped onto code that exact-text search could not find.

The team also found that agents preferred familiar operations, such as text search, file reads, and symbol lookup, over higher-level abstractions that required extra verification, so tool design mattered as much as the index. The practical question for a team is whether its agents' failures come from ambiguous requirements or from simple lookups, since that decides whether an index is worth its overhead.

item.title: DeepMind's AlphaGenome 2 finds nearly twice as many gene-expression variants as its predecessor
item.description:
Trained on more than 100 million cell profiles across 68 tissues, the model is available now for non-commercial research through an API.

DeepMind has released AlphaGenome 2, the follow-up to its variant-effect model. The first version worked at the level of broad tissue averages. Some variant effects only show up in specific cells and get averaged away in tissue-wide models, and the new version targets those. On DeepMind's tally, the new model flags close to double the expression-altering variants its predecessor found.

Training drew on over 100 million single-cell profiles spanning 68 tissues. DeepMind argues that this lets the model predict variant effects in disease-relevant cells, as well as in cell and disease states it never saw in training. The first model spread one model's capacity across thousands of experiments, which made closely related cell types hard to tell apart, so the redesign handles cell types explicitly.

Access is limited for now. AlphaGenome 2 is available for non-commercial research through the AlphaGenome API and is in private preview for commercial research. The figures are DeepMind's own, so independent benchmarks on held-out variants will be the real test of whether the added detail improves disease research.

item.title: IBM plans a 500-plus qubit Nighthawk processor and cuts its linked systems to two
item.description:
IBM still aims for error-corrected machines before the decade ends, and it is pairing a general-purpose processor track with an error-correction track.

IBM used its Quantum Developer's Conference to update its roadmap. The Nighthawk line of general-purpose processors gains a version with more than 500 programmable qubits, and IBM plans to offer access to a dual-processor system in 2027 by linking two 520-qubit chips before that year ends. It has also dropped its plan to link Nighthawk processors in groups of nine, cutting the intended number to two. The total qubit count planned for next year is unchanged; what changes is how IBM gets there.

The roadmap runs on two tracks. One builds the hardware needed for error-corrected machines, which requires specific qubit layouts plus extra qubits for operations, so it may not be useful on its own. The other delivers Nighthawk processors for people testing algorithms today. IBM credits hardware-based qubit resets, introduced in the generation released in September, with a performance gain.

Nighthawk started with 120 qubits and roughly 5,000 gate operations before errors make the output unreliable. Through 2028 the public track will bring only revisions of that generation. The open question is whether IBM can keep its error-correction timetable while the general-purpose line widens.

item.title: Ukrainian strikes permanently destroyed 2.84% of Yandex Cloud customer data
item.description:
Yandex says customers who had enabled its backup tools lost nothing, which makes the lack of backup copies the central lesson.

Russia's Yandex says 2.84% of customer data was permanently lost after Ukrainian strikes on data centres in the country. The company says recovery is impossible because of critical damage to equipment and because the platform held no backup copies for the affected data. Customers who had enabled the platform's backup tools reportedly lost nothing. Yandex says it is revising its approach to data protection and disaster recovery. This account comes from the headline and standfirst only, because the full article could not be retrieved, so the affected services and the timeline are unconfirmed here.
